newsitem.title: USA: SEC probe of DC finances ongoing, expanding - lawyer.
newsitem.headline: SEC probe of DC finances ongoing, expanding - lawyer.

text.p: An SEC probe of a December 1994 District of Columbia note sale continues and probably has been expanded to cover city financial statements for fiscal year 1995, the D.C. control board's lawyer said.

"The District sold a large amount of bonds in" late 1994, Daniel Rezneck, general counsel for the five-member control board said. "The result was a Securities and Exchange Commission investigation of the District which is still going on."

Rezneck added that D.C. auditor KPMG Peat Marwick in January highlighted deficiencies in D.C.'s financial statements for FY 1995. Those recent findings are "undoubtedly part of SEC's investigation," Rezneck said.
He added, however, SEC probably would not be investigating the city as enthusiastically if D.C. were not at its doorstep.

"One of the drawbacks of being located where we are is that when federal agencies have their own budgets cut, as the SEC has, it's very tempting to take it out on the District because it doesn't cost much," said Rezneck, who was speaking at a D.C. Bar meeting.

"You don't have to pay travel expenses. I'm not saying they don't have a case, but the fact is if we were 1,000 miles away, I suspect they might not be (proceeding) with the same enthusiasm," Rezneck said.
"They get a bigger bang for the buck, and we have to pay for it," Rezneck said.
SEC in February 1995 subpoenaed financial information from the District and then-auditor Coopers & Lybrand.
Washington sources said SEC was examining financial disclosures by the city for its December 1994 $250 million short-term note sale.

When the notes were sold through a syndicate led by Prudential Securities Inc., bond documents estimated a D.C. budget deficit at $492 million. Six weeks later, however, city officials placed the deficit at roughly $722 million.
"That occasion turned into kind of a disastrous situation," Rezneck said.

But he said the city has neatly rebounded with two recent offerings, a $220 million short term note sale last summer and last week's brisk sale of $168.8 million in 20-year general obligation bonds to a syndicated headed by Merrill Lynch & Co.
"We've been able to sell securities at very good interest rates" even though D.C. bonds still get junk bond ratings and no insurer will insure them, Rezneck said.
The reason is the hard work of the D.C. control board and the city's chief financial officer Anthony Williams.

"When you have to look at these squinty-eyed characters on Wall Street who are deciding whether to invest in D.C. securities, the credibility of (the city's) numbers is awfully important," Rezneck said.
Rezneck said the SEC's probe of D.C. is not an "isolated" incident. "The SEC's had a campaign recently about fraud in the sale of municipal securities," he said.
The commission reached a settlement with Maricopa County, Ariz. last week, but it decided it did not have a case against the city of Denver, he said.
